title: Node GPU Failure Triage and Capacity Handbook (draft)
content:
Purpose:
This doc is a pragmatic SRE handbook for triaging node-level GPU failures, executing safe cordon/drain workflows, performing hardware swaps (RMA), and injecting capacity to reduce customer impact. It is intentionally concise — step-first with checks and short commands for on-call use.

Scope and assumptions:
- Target environment: k8s clusters running Redwood serving runtime (gpu-enabled nodes).
- Assumes standard node labels: node.kubernetes.io/gpu=true and taint: infra/gpu-maintenance:NoSchedule used for maintenance.
- There are spare nodes in the capacity pool or a documented autoscaler path.
- This doc covers: triage -> cordon/drain -> mitigate traffic -> hardware replacement acceptance -> node re-join -> capacity add and post-incident follow-up.

Quick triage checklist (first 10 minutes):
- Confirm impact: dashboards (token latency, error rates, queue length), per-model SLOs.
- Identify affected pods: kubectl get pods -A -o wide | grep <node-name>
- Check node health: kubectl describe node <node> ; dmesg | tail on node (if SSH available) to spot kernel oops, ECC errors, or PCI errors.
- Check GPU device: ssh node -> nvidia-smi -q (timeout vs not-present). If driver not responding, assume hardware or driver crash.
- Check kubelet status: systemctl status kubelet ; journalctl -u kubelet -n 200
- Post a Slack update to #sre-oncall: minimal: incident id, node, customer-facing impact, next action (cordon & drain planned?).

Safe cordon and drain (minimize model disruptions):
- Goal: move pods safely off node, prefer graceful eviction for model-serving pods that can reconnect.
- Commands:
  - kubectl annotate node <node> maintenance.sre/redwood=true --overwrite
  - kubectl cordon <node>
  - kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --grace-period=60 --force --timeout=15m
Notes and gotchas:
- If pods have PDBs blocking eviction, either wait or temporarily increment PDB to allow drain (coord with product if needed).
- For long-lived KV cache pods: prefer to scale up replicas elsewhere first before eviction. Example: scale deployment foo --replicas X+1 then wait for readiness.
- If drain hangs on terminating pods: kubectl get pod -n <ns> <pod> -o yaml to inspect finalizers. If safe, remove finalizer. Use as last resort.

Traffic mitigation and routing fallbacks:
- If draining causes capacity dip, engage routing policy to route to fallback model variants or lower-cost regions: follow Console -> Rollouts -> Pause traffic to cluster -> Enable fallback. (Refer to Console playbook)
- If using smart routing: temporarily pin the model route to Dedicated pool or bigger instance sizes.

Hardware replacement (high-level):
- If node confirmed hardware GPU fault (RMA):
  1) Open RMA ticket with vendor (include serial, nvidia-smi output, node logs).
  2) Mark node as under-hardware-replacement: kubectl label node <node> repair=schedule --overwrite
  3) If replacement is physical on-prem: follow data center checklist (safety, ESD, bring replacement kit).
  4) After install: run driver + runtime validation.

Acceptance tests after GPU install / driver re-install:
- On-node checks (as root):
  - modprobe nvidia || journalctl -k | grep -i nvidia
  - systemctl restart nvidia-docker || systemctl restart containerd/docker (depending on runtime)
  - nvidia-smi --query-gpu=name,uuid,driver_version,memory.total --format=csv
  - run quick GPU micro-bench: python3 /opt/recovery/gpu-smoke.py --duration 30s (small torch cuda kernel)
- Kube re-join: kubelet should register the node automatically; if not: systemctl start kubelet && journalctl -u kubelet -f to watch registration.
- Once node shows Ready and label node.kubernetes.io/gpu=true present, remove repair label: kubectl label node <node> repair-

Post-join cluster checks and traffic rebalancing:
- Confirm pods scheduling: kubectl get pods -o wide --all-namespaces | grep <node>
- Confirm serving health: hit health endpoints for model-serving pods scheduled on node (400s vs 200).
- Remove cordon: kubectl uncordon <node>
- Allow autoscaler to rebalance; if manual, scale workloads down/back to normal and ensure no resource contention.

Capacity add (when cluster-level capacity shortfall detected):
- If autoscaler exists: increase node group desired count (cloud console or terraform pipeline) or trigger emergency scale (runbook SOP: run terraform apply -var=emergency_scale=true).
- If manual add: provision node(s) from inventory, bootstrap with image, join cluster using kubeadm/auto-bootstrap pipeline.
- Perform smoke tests on new node: nvidia-smi, driver check, kubelet register, run small model containers to verify inference path.
- If using reserved capacity pools: move routing to the reserved pool until new nodes are healthy.

Troubleshooting quick hits (common root causes):
- GPU ECC errors -> likely hardware aging; check vendor telemetry and RMA.
- Driver mismatch after kernel update -> roll kernel or recompile driver.
- NVidia MIG misconfig -> ensure correct MIG profile applied if in use.
- Container runtime OOM or GPU allocation fail -> check device-plugin logs and CRI runtime plugin (nvidia-container-runtime).

Rollback / emergency fallback:
- If reintroducing node causes regression: cordon immediately and roll back node to previous known-good image.
- If traffic still unhealthy: change rollout to previous model version (Console rollouts) and open incident escalation.

Escalation matrix (contacts):
- Oncall SRE (first responder): assigned via PagerDuty
- SRE Lead: Marcus Lee (pager)
- Infra Eng (hardware vendor escalations): Daniel Park
- Platform Eng (autoscaler / terraform): Aisha Khan
- Slack channels: #sre-oncall, #infra-hardware, #platform-ops

Post-incident follow-up (within 48–72 hours):
- Timeline: collect timestamps for detection, cordon, drain start/finish, node out-of-service, RMA shipped/received, node back online. Attach to JIRA incident ticket.
- Root cause analysis: create a short RCA doc with contributing factors, mitigation status, long-term fixes. Tag product owners for customer impact.
- Runbook updates: add any edge-case steps discovered (e.g., device-plugin restart order, extra driver flags).
- Inventory & spares: log spare GPUs used, reorder if below threshold.

Notes-to-self / open questions:
- Should we default to evacuation order: KV cache pods first, then model replicas? (proposal: prefer least-disruptive ordering; document exact ordering per cluster in a follow-up)
- Consider adding an automated node-health-playbook that runs a basic nvidia-smi/micro-benchmark and taints node if failing health checks.

Appendix: useful commands (copy-paste friendly)
- kubectl cordon <node>
- kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --grace-period=60 --timeout=15m
- kubectl uncordon <node>
- kubectl label node <node> repair=schedule --overwrite
- ssh root@<node> "nvidia-smi -q"
- journalctl -u kubelet -n 400 | sed -n '1,200p'

References and links:
- Confluence: infra/gpu-hardware-guides
- GitHub: github.com/redwood-inference/cluster-ops (bootstrap scripts)
- JIRA template: SRE-INCIDENT-TEMPLATE

End of handbook (draft). This is intentionally terse; please add specific per-cluster quirks below or in comments.

-- Leila
